    print("✓ Test 1: Empty dict DataFrame has RangeIndex columns")
    
    # Test 2: Empty dict with explicit index
    df2 = pd.DataFrame({}, index=[1, 2, 3])
    assert isinstance(df2.columns, pd.RangeIndex), f"Expected RangeIndex, got {type(df2.columns)}"
    assert len(df2.columns) == 0, f"Expected 0 columns, got {len(df2.columns)}"
    print("✓ Test 2: Empty dict DataFrame with index has RangeIndex columns")
    
    # Test 3: Empty dict with explicit columns (should still use provided columns)
    df3 = pd.DataFrame({}, columns=['a', 'b'])
    assert isinstance(df3.columns, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(df3.columns)}"
    assert len(df3.columns) == 2, f"Expected 2 columns, got {len(df3.columns)}"
    assert list(df3.columns) == ['a', 'b'], f"Expected ['a', 'b'], got {list(df3.columns)}"
    print("✓ Test 3: Empty dict DataFrame with explicit columns uses provided columns")
    
    # Test 4: Empty dict with RangeIndex columns
    df4 = pd.DataFrame({}, columns=pd.RangeIndex(0, 3))
    assert isinstance(df4.columns, pd.RangeIndex), f"Expected RangeIndex, got {type(df4.columns)}"
    assert len(df4.columns) == 3, f"Expected 3 columns, got {len(df4.columns)}"
    print("✓ Test 4: Empty dict DataFrame with RangeIndex columns")
    
    # Test 5: Non-empty dict (regression test)
    df5 = pd.DataFrame({'x': [1, 2], 'y': [3, 4]})
    assert isinstance(df5.columns, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(df5.columns)}"
    assert len(df5.columns) == 2, f"Expected 2 columns, got {len(df5.columns)}"
    assert list(df5.columns) == ['x', 'y'], f"Expected ['x', 'y'], got {list(df5.columns)}"
    print("✓ Test 5: Non-empty dict DataFrame uses Index for columns")
    
    # Test 6: Dict with empty arrays
    df6 = pd.DataFrame({'a': [], 'b': []})
    assert isinstance(df6.columns, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(df6.columns)}"
    assert len(df6.columns) == 2, f"Expected 2 columns, got {len(df6.columns)}"
    assert list(df6.columns) == ['a', 'b'], f"Expected ['a', 'b'], got {list(df6.columns)}"
    print("✓ Test 6: Dict with empty arrays uses Index for columns")
    
    # Test 7: Dict with single empty array
    df7 = pd.DataFrame({'single': []})
    assert isinstance(df7.columns, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(df7.columns)}"
    assert len(df7.columns) == 1, f"Expected 1 column, got {len(df7.columns)}"
    assert list(df7.columns) == ['single'], f"Expected ['single'], got {list(df7.columns)}"
    print("✓ Test 7: Dict with single empty array uses Index for columns")
    
    # Test 8: Dict with None values
    df8 = pd.DataFrame({'a': None, 'b': None})
    assert isinstance(df8.columns, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(df8.columns)}"
    assert len(df8.columns) == 2, f"Expected 2 columns, got {len(df8.columns)}"
    assert list(df8.columns) == ['a', 'b'], f"Expected ['a', 'b'], got {list(df8.columns)}"
    print("✓ Test 8: Dict with None values uses Index for columns")
    
    # Test 9: Dict with mixed types
    df9 = pd.DataFrame({'str': ['a', 'b'], 'int': [1, 2], 'float': [1.1, 2.2]})
    assert isinstance(df9.columns, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(df9.columns)}"
    assert len(df9.columns) == 3, f"Expected 3 columns, got {len(df9.columns)}"
    print("✓ Test 9: Dict with mixed types uses Index for columns")
    
    # Test 10: Dict with numeric keys
    df10 = pd.DataFrame({1: [1, 2], 2: [3, 4]})
    assert isinstance(df10.columns, pd.Index), f"Expected Index, got {type(df10.columns)}"
    assert len(df10.columns) == 2, f"Expected 2 columns, got {len(df10.columns)}"
    assert list(df10.columns) == [1, 2], f"Expected [1, 2], got {list(df10.columns)}"
    print("✓ Test 10: Dict with numeric keys uses Index for columns")
    
    print("\n🎉 All edge case tests passed!")

if __name__ == "__main__":

## Problem Analysis
The issue was that `infer_freq` was throwing a TypeError when given a `Series` of timezone-aware `Timestamp`s, even though it worked correctly with `DatetimeIndex` of the same data. 1. **Added import**: Added `is_datetime64tz_dtype` to the imports from `pandas.core.dtypes.common`

The specific changes were:
- Line 35: Added `is_datetime64tz_dtype` to the import statement
- Lines 152-157: Added `or is_datetime64tz_dtype(values)` to the dtype validation condition

import pandas as pd
from pandas.api.types import is_categorical_dtype

def test_sparse_categorical_dtype():
    """Test the issue with is_categorical_dtype and Sparse[category, nan]"""
    
    # Create a sparse categorical series
    s = pd.Series(
        ["a", "b", "c", "a", "b", "c"],
        dtype=pd.SparseDtype(pd.CategoricalDtype(['a', 'b', 'c']))
    )
    
    print("Series dtype:", s.dtype)
    print("is_categorical_dtype(s):", is_categorical_dtype(s))
    print("Expected: True")
    
    # Test direct dtype check
    print("is_categorical_dtype(s.dtype):", is_categorical_dtype(s.dtype))
    print("Expected: True")
    
    # Test with regular categorical for comparison
    s_regular = pd.Series(
        ["a", "b", "c", "a", "b", "c"],
        dtype=pd.CategoricalDtype(['a', 'b', 'c'])
    )
    
    print("\nRegular categorical:")
    print("Series dtype:", s_regular.dtype)
    print("is_categorical_dtype(s_regular):", is_categorical_dtype(s_regular))
    print("Expected: True")
    
    # Test unsigned integer sparse case (should work)
    s_uint = pd.Series(
        [0, 1, 2, 3],
        name="pd_unsigned_integer",
        dtype=pd.SparseDtype(pd.UInt8Dtype(), pd.NA)
    )
    
    print("\nSparse unsigned integer:")
    print("Series dtype:", s_uint.dtype)
    from pandas.api.types import is_unsigned_integer_dtype
    print("is_unsigned_integer_dtype(s_uint):", is_unsigned_integer_dtype(s_uint))
    print("Expected: True")
    
    # Assert expected behavior
    assert is_categorical_dtype(s_regular), "Regular categorical should return True"
    assert is_unsigned_integer_dtype(s_uint), "Sparse unsigned integer should return True"
    
    # This should pass after the fix
    try:
        assert is_categorical_dtype(s), "Sparse categorical should return True"
        print("\n✅ Test PASSED: Sparse categorical dtype correctly identified")
    except AssertionError:
        print("\n❌ Test FAILED: Sparse categorical dtype not correctly identified")
        return False
    
    return True

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_sparse_categorical_dtype()</parameter>

BUG: Inconsistent dtype selection for row-wise(`axis=1`) operations in `pandas-2.0` for `datetime` & `timedelta` dtypes
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
In [2]: import pandas as pd

In [3]: from io import StringIO

In [4]: csv_str = ',t1,t2\n0,2020-08-01 09:00:00,1940-08-31 06:00:00\n1,1920-05-01 10:30:00,2020-08-02 10:00:00\n'

In [5]: df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv_str))

In [6]: df = df[['t1', 't2']]

In [7]: df['t1'] = df['t1'].astype('datetime64[us]')

In [8]: df['t2'] = df['t2'].astype('datetime64[us]')

In [9]: df
Out[9]: 
                   t1                  t2
0 2020-08-01 09:00:00 1940-08-31 06:00:00
1 1920-05-01 10:30:00 2020-08-02 10:00:00

In [10]: df.max(axis=1)
Out[10]: 
0   2020-08-01 09:00:00
1   2020-08-02 10:00:00
dtype: datetime64[us]

In [11]: df['t2'] = df['t2'].astype('datetime64[ms]')

In [12]: df.dtypes
Out[12]: 
t1    datetime64[us]
t2    datetime64[ms]
dtype: object

In [13]: df.max(axis=1)
Out[13]: 
0   2020-08-01 09:00:00
1   2020-08-02 10:00:00
dtype: datetime64[ns]
```


### Issue Description

In the above example, a row-wise operation on different time resolutions seems to be defaulting to `ns` time resolution, whereas here we can clearly choose to return `datetime64[us]`(the lowest possible time resolution depending on the operation performed-`min`).

### Expected Behavior

```python
In [13]: df.max(axis=1)
Out[13]: 
0   2020-08-01 09:00:00
1   2020-08-02 10:00:00
dtype: datetime64[us]
```

  <parameter=result>I have successfully implemented a fix for the inconsistent dtype selection issue for row-wise operations with datetime and timedelta dtypes in pandas 2.0.

## Summary of Changes

The issue was in the `find_common_type` function in `/testbed/pandas/core/dtypes/cast.py`. The original code was hardcoded to always return `datetime64[ns]` or `timedelta64[ns]` for datetime/timedelta types, regardless of the actual resolutions of the input dtypes.

## Root Cause
The problem was on lines 1410-1421 where the function was using:
```python
# take lowest unit
if all(is_datetime64_dtype(t) for t in types):
    return np.dtype("datetime64[ns]")
if all(is_timedelta64_dtype(t) for t in types):
    return np.dtype("timedelta64[ns]")
```

This always returned nanosecond resolution, ignoring the actual resolutions of the input dtypes.

## Solution
I replaced the hardcoded resolution with logic that properly determines the coarsest resolution among the input datetime/timedelta types:

```python
# take lowest unit for datetime/timedelta types
if all(is_datetime64_dtype(t) for t in types):
    # Find the coarsest resolution among datetime64 types
    units = [t.str.split('[')[1].split(']')[0] for t in types]
    unit_precedence = {'ns': 0, 'us': 1, 'ms': 2, 's': 3}
    coarsest_unit = min(units, key=lambda x: unit_precedence.get(x, 0))
    return np.dtype(f"datetime64[{coarsest_unit}]")
if all(is_timedelta64_dtype(t) for t in types):
    # Find the coarsest resolution among timedelta64 types
    units = [t.str.split('[')[1].split(']')[0] for t in types]
    unit_precedence = {'ns': 0, 'us': 1, 'ms': 2, 's': 3}
    coarsest_unit = min(units, key=lambda x: unit_precedence.get(x, 0))
    return np.dtype(f"timedelta64[{coarsest_unit}]")
```

## Verification
The fix has been verified to:
1. Resolve the original issue described in the GitHub issue
2. Correctly handle multiple datetime/timedelta resolutions
3. Return the coarsest resolution (e.g., `datetime64[us]` when mixing `us` and `ms`)
4. Maintain backward compatibility for single-resolution cases
5. Pass existing unit tests

The reproduction script now shows the expected behavior where `df.max(axis=1)` returns `datetime64[us]` instead of `datetime64[ns]` when mixing different datetime resolutions.</parameter>

<github_issue>
API: value-dependent behaviour in concat with all-NA data
In general, we want to get rid of value-dependent behaviour in concat-operations: the resulting dtype of a concat-operation only depends on the input *dtypes*, and not on the exact content (the exact values) of the inputs. 

This has been discussed in the past on general occasions, eg in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/33607 when adding the general EA interface for concat (there is still one value-dependent special case for Categorical involving integer categories / missing values, encoded in `core/dtypes/concat.py::cast_to_common_type`), or https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/39122 about this issue when concerning empty series/dataframes. 

But so one other case (which came up recently in eg https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/39574 and https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/39612) is related to all-NA/NaN objects. 

For DataFrames, when there is all-missing column, its type gets ignored when determining the result dtype (which, however, requires inspecting the values of the column). Small example:

```python
>>> df_missing = pd.DataFrame({'a': [np.nan]})
>>> df_dt64 = pd.DataFrame({'a': [pd.Timestamp("2021-01-01")]}, dtype="datetime64[ns]")

>>> pd.concat([df_missing, df_dt64])
           a
0        NaT
0 2021-01-01

>>> pd.concat([df_missing, df_dt64]).dtypes
a    datetime64[ns]
dtype: object
```

This can be useful, as you can get such object/float dtype columns depending on how those "empty" all-NaN DataFrames are created (eg when constructing a DataFrame with given index/column but without data, or by reindexing the rows of an actual empty DataFrame, or reindexing the columns of a non-empty DataFrame).

However, it does introduce annoying value-dependent behaviour, and is also not very consistent throughout pandas. For example, Series does not check for this, and will actually result in object dtype:

```python
>>> pd.concat([df_missing['a'], df_dt64['a']])
0                    NaN
0    2021-01-01 00:00:00
Name: a, dtype: object
```

Further, this is also not consistent across data types. For example, we don't check for all-NA for the new nullable dtypes.

For ArrayManager, I didn't yet implement any special case value-dependent behaviour (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/39612, so on this aspect it diverges from the BlockManager behaviour), as it would be good to first decide on the desired behaviour long term.

"""

import pandas as pd

    """Test DataFrame concat with all-NA column - should NOT ignore all-NA types."""
    print("=== DataFrame concat test (FIXED) ===")
    
    df_missing = pd.DataFrame({'a': [np.nan]})
    df_dt64 = pd.DataFrame({'a': [pd.Timestamp("2021-01-01")]}, dtype="datetime64[ns]")
    
    print("df_missing dtypes:", df_missing.dtypes)
    print("df_dt64 dtypes:", df_dt64.dtypes)
    
    result = pd.concat([df_missing, df_dt64])
    print("concat result dtypes:", result.dtypes)
    print("concat result:")
    print(result)
    
    # After fix: should be object dtype (not value-dependent)
    expected_dtype = "object"
    actual_dtype = str(result.dtypes['a'])
    print(f"Expected dtype: {expected_dtype}")
    print(f"Actual dtype: {actual_dtype}")
    print(f"Fix successful: {actual_dtype == expected_dtype}")
    print()

def test_series_concat_all_na_fixed():
    """Test Series concat with all-NA data - should remain consistent."""

    s_missing = pd.Series([np.nan], name='a')
    s_dt64 = pd.Series([pd.Timestamp("2021-01-01")], dtype="datetime64[ns]", name='a')

    print("s_dt64 dtype:", s_dt64.dtype)

    actual_dtype = str(result.dtype)
    print(f"Expected dtype: {expected_dtype}")
    print(f"Actual dtype: {actual_dtype}")
    print(f"Behavior consistent: {actual_dtype == expected_dtype}")
    print()

def test_edge_cases():
    """Test edge cases to ensure robustness."""
    print("=== Edge cases test ===")
    
    # Test with multiple all-NA columns
    df1 = pd.DataFrame({'a': [np.nan, np.nan], 'b': [1, 2]})

    print()

def test_empty_generator():
    """Test with empty generator"""
    print("Testing empty generator...")
    idx = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([(1, 2), (3, 4)])

    """Test with single tuple generator"""

    expected = np.array([True, False])
